previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with type 1 diabetes, chronic back pain, and a history of H. pylori gastritis was readmitted for persistent nausea, vomiting, and worsening back pain after an incomplete recovery from a recent hospitalization. She presented with elevated glucose of 444, which resolved with IV fluids and her home insulin regimen without evidence of ketoacidosis. A gastric biopsy revealed active gastritis with findings suggestive of H. pylori, explaining her gastrointestinal symptoms, while a gastric emptying study was normal, ruling out gastroparesis. She was treated with IV Zofran, continued on metoclopramide and omeprazole, and her pain was initially managed with Dilaudid before transitioning to acetaminophen, ibuprofen, and cyclobenzaprine. Her nausea resolved, she tolerated a regular diet, and her vitals stabilized. Sertraline was increased to 150mg daily for depression, and close primary care follow-up was arranged. She was discharged home in stable condition with updated medications and instructions for ongoing symptom management.

# N/V: The patient had been started on triple therapy for H. 
pylori the day before admission. This was held during admission 
and the patient was initially started on an IV PPI. Her home 
Reglan was also initially given IV. Zofran 4mg IV q 4 hours PRN 
until vomiting improved. Given vomiting and tachcardia, gave IVF 
until patient able to tolerate at least clears po. Urine culture 
was negative. Diet was advanced as tolerated and medications 
were switched to po. Nutrition saw and discussed food choices 
with the patient. Patient had initially improved, but after 
being advanced to a full diet, began to start vomiting again. 
KUB showed stool, but no signs of obstruction. GI was consulted. 
They recommended stool cultures that were still pending at the 
time of discharge, as well as some imaging. UGI series showed 
reflux and otherwise normal gut motility, but the small bowel 
follow through was not entirely completed as the patient began 
to vomit during the study. LFTs were normal, and RUQ US did not 
show any biliary tract disease. CT AP with contrast was ordered, 
but patient was unable to tolerate the barium. The patient 
stated she having more of her low back pain than abdominal pain. 
Her bowel regimen was increased and narcotic pain medications 
were held. The patient's nausea improved after having a bowel 
movement. On the day of discharge, patient was tolerating a 
regular diet and had not vomited for 24 hours. She was 
discharged on a PPI but without further H pylori treatment. Abx 
will be discussed when she goes for her GI follow up 
appointment. Stool studies can be followed up by GI and/or PCP.

taken and FSG readings throughout the day. She will be 
discharged home with 20 units of Lantus and instructions to keep 
track of her sugars at home so this dose can potentially be 
adjusted at PCP follow up.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___,

Thank you for coming to ___ for your medical care. You were 
admitted to the hospital for nausea and vomiting. We gave you IV 
fluids as well as medicines for pain and nausea. We gave you 
food to eat slowly. Your nausea and pain improved. We asked the 
___ doctors to ___ you. You had some tests that did not show 
any problems with your liver or gallbladder or any obstruction 
in your digestive tract. You have an appointment to follow up 
with the GI doctors, and at that visit how to treat the H. 
pylori infection in your stomach can be discussed.    

We made the following changes to your medication:
- Please START taking Zofran (ondansetron) 4mg by mouth every 8 
hours as needed for nausea. 
- Please START taking Senna 1 tablet and docusate 100mg twice a 
day. Please stop taking these medicines if you have loose 
stools. 
- Please START taking bisacodyl 10mg daily if you have not had a 
bowel movement in 2 days. 
- CHANGE your metoclopramide (Reglan) to 10 mg with meals and at 
bedtime.
- Please DECREASE your Lantus to 20 units each night. You should 
check your blood sugars when you wake up in the morning and 2 
hours after you eat. Keep a record of these sugars and bring 
them when you see your primary care doctor so your insulin can 
be adjusted if need be. 
- Please STOP taking the amoxacillin and clarithromycin that 
were prescribed for the H. pylori infection for now. The GI 
doctors ___ these medicines or change them when you see 
them.

of nausea and vomiting.  Evaluate for evidence of obstruction.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:  Supine and upright views of the abdomen are submitted for review. 
There are no dilated bowel loops identified, with air and stool seen extending
to the rectum.  Moderate amount of retained colonic fecal material is present.
There is no pneumatosis, bowel wall thickening, or evidence of free air.  No
abnormal tissue calcifications or soft tissue masses are identified. 
Visualized osseous structures are normal.  The lung bases are clear.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of obstruction.  Moderate retained fecal material
within the colon.

INDICATION:  A ___ female with recurrent nausea and vomiting.

COMPARISON:  Abdomen CT ___ and abdomen ultrasound, ___.

FINDINGS:  The liver shows no focal or textural abnormality.  No biliary
dilatation is seen and the common duct measures 0.2 cm.  The gallbladder is
normal with no gallstones identified.  No gallbladder wall edema or
pericholecystic fluid is seen.  The portal vein is patent with hepatopetal
flow.  The pancreas is unremarkable.  No ascites is seen in the right upper
quadrant.

IMPRESSION:  Normal right upper quadrant ultrasound with no findings to
suggest the cause of the patient's nausea and vomiting.

CLINICAL INDICATION:  ___ female with type 1 diabetes mellitus and
recurrent nausea and vomiting.  Evaluate for dysmotility or proximal bowel
obstruction.

COMPARISON:  None available.

DOUBLE CONTRAST UPPER GI:  Barium passes freely to the stomach.  No tertiary
contractions are seen.  No hiatal hernia is seen.  However, there was free
reflux to the upper esophagus during the exam.  Limited views of the stomach
appear normal.  The duodenum demonstrates a normal course with spontaneous
passage of barium into the proximal jejunum.  Delayed spot film demonstrates
passage of contrast into the small bowel in the left lower quadrant.  The
patient subsequently vomited barium and requested to terminate the study;
therefore, a full small bowel follow-through was not performed.  This was
discussed with Dr. ___ at 4:30 p.m. on ___ who agreed with
the plan to terminate the study.
